This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

Christmas and Easter are the two biggest points of my year — I spend weeks getting ready for them with family and church, and Lent before Easter is 40 days of fasting that always makes me think about forgiveness and how I treat people. Do you think going through the same thing every year changes how someone thinks about what they owe others?

It’s beautiful that you let those seasons become a kind of “reset button” for your heart and your relationships. The fact that you’re already noticing a shift in how you think about what you owe others shows that the rituals are doing something deeper than just decoration or celebration. --- ## 1. Rituals as a mirror for our values When we repeat a practice—whether it’s lighting a candle on Christmas Eve, attending a special Mass on Easter, or counting the days of Lent—our minds are given a frame to reflect on what matters most. The repetition does two things: | What the ritual does | Why it matters | |----------------------|----------------| | **Creates a pause** | We step out of the day‑to‑day rush and give space to think about priorities. | | **Reinforces a narrative** | The story of sacrifice, renewal, or generosity becomes part of our identity. | | **Signals intention** | By setting aside time for fasting or giving, we signal to ourselves and others that we’re committed to those values. | Because the same story is told each year, the narrative becomes a touchstone. It’s like a compass that points you back to the same core questions: “What do I owe to my family? To my community? To myself?” --- ## 2. How repetition can shift the “owe” mindset ### a. From obligation to gratitude - **Obligation** is often framed as “I have to give because I’m supposed to.” - **Gratitude** reframes it as “I want to give because I’m thankful for what I’ve received.” When Lent or Christmas becomes a ritual of giving, the language shifts. The act of fasting or donating is no longer a duty; it’s a choice that reflects appreciation. Over time, that choice can become a habit of generosity rather than a chore. ### b. From guilt to forgiveness - **Guilt** can arise when we feel we haven’t met an expectation (e.g., “I didn’t give enough this year”). - **Forgiveness** is the act of letting go of that self‑judgment and recognizing that we’re human. The 40 days of Lent, for instance, are a reminder that we’re all in the same process of growth. The ritual invites us to look inward, acknowledge our shortcomings, and then extend that same compassion outward—to others who may be struggling. ### c. From routine to intentionality Repetition can make a practice feel automatic, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing. The key is to keep the *intentionality* alive: - **Ask yourself** each year: “What new lesson can I learn from this season?” - **Set a small, specific goal** (e.g., “This year, I’ll volunteer at the soup kitchen once a month”). - **Reflect afterward**: What did I feel? What did I notice about my relationships? When you add a layer of reflection, the ritual stops becoming a checkbox and becomes a living conversation with yourself and the people you love. --- ## 3. Practical ways to keep the “owe” mindset evolving | Strategy | How it works | Example | |----------|--------------|---------| | **Journaling** | Write a short note after each major event. | “I felt grateful when my niece shared her homemade cookies.” | | **Accountability partner** | Share your intentions with a trusted friend or family member. | “I’ll give a meal to someone in need; let’s check in next month.” | | **Mindful giving** | Before you give, pause and ask, “Why am I giving this?” | “I’m giving this donation because I want to support the community that helped me.” | | **Celebrate small wins** | Acknowledge even the modest acts of kindness. | “I listened to my sister’s story without interrupting.” | --- ## 4. A gentle reminder It’s natural for the rhythm of the seasons to feel familiar, but that familiarity can be a powerful ally. Each year, you’re given a chance to: 1. **Revisit the story** you’re living (sacrifice, renewal, generosity). 2. **Reassess your commitments** to others and to yourself. 3. **Adjust the scale** of your “owe”—whether it’s more time, more empathy, or more tangible support. You’re already on a path that many find transformative. By staying curious and intentional, you’ll keep the seasons from becoming just another calendar event and instead let them be a living dialogue with the people you love and the values you cherish. --- ### A thought to carry with you > “Each year, the same candle is lit, but the light it casts can grow brighter or dimmer depending on how we choose to hold it.” May your celebrations, fasts, and reflections continue to illuminate the ways you give, forgive, and grow. If you’d like to explore specific ways to deepen any of these practices, I’m here to help.
